source: Tran and Kiela (2026) Single-Agent LLMs Outperform Multi-Agent Systems on Multi-Hop Reasoning Under Equal Thinking Token Budgets
finding: With thinking tokens matched, one agent matches or beats five multi-agent designs on multi-hop QA. Multi-agent only wins at 100 tokens or when context is corrupted.
numbers: FRAMES and MuSiQue (4-hop); Qwen3-30B-A3B, R1-Distill-Llama-70B, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Gemini-2.5-Pro; 8 panels. Mean accuracy at 1000 tokens: single 0.418, sequential 0.379, subtask-parallel 0.369, parallel-roles 0.381, debate 0.388, ensemble 0.333. At 5000: single 0.427, debate 0.420, roles 0.417, ensemble 0.411. At 100 tokens: debate 0.370 and sequential 0.364 beat single 0.290 (no useful trace at 100). Corruption test (Qwen3, 1000 tokens, masking or substitution at alpha 0.7): sequential beat single.
quote: SAS is the strongest default architecture for multi-hop reasoning.
limits: Text-only multi-hop QA; no tools; Gemini token counts approximate; corruption values only in a figure; LLM judge. Two benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and 4: at equal tokens a single agent is the default; add agents only when context is degraded or the budget is tiny.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems (budget and threshold details, full text re-read)
finding: Kim's design is already token-matched. The 45% single-agent threshold is a within-sample rule, not tested on outside tasks.
numbers: All systems matched for total reasoning tokens (mean 4,800 per trial) and tool access. Capability-ceiling beta -0.236, p=.004. Threshold achieves 94% match rate by binomial test. SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench use 20-instance subsets; bootstrap 95% CI width about 20 points per cell; other benchmarks 50-100 instances.
quote: coordination yields diminishing returns beyond 45% single-agent baselines
limits: Matching splits a fixed budget so each agent gets less (authors' own mechanism); per-cell comparisons underpowered at n=20; threshold fitted on the same six benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: the penalty on multi-agent comes from budget fragmentation, which is real under equal tokens. Threshold is a heuristic prior, not a law.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think
finding: Traces from current reasoning models often omit the hint that actually changed the answer. They are useful evidence but not a complete audit trail.
numbers: Claude 3.7 Sonnet 25% and DeepSeek R1 39% faithfulness averaged over MMLU and GPQA. Misaligned hints: 20% and 29%. GPQA faithfulness lower by relative 44% (Claude) and 32% (R1). Outcome RL: +63% relative on MMLU, +41% on GPQA, then plateau near 28% and 20%. RL reward hacks exploited on over 99% of examples within 30 steps; hack verbalised on under 2% of examples in 5 of 6 environments.
limits: Hint-based test only measures faithfulness to inserted hints; Claude 3.5, 3.7 and DeepSeek V3, R1 only.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: a scratch trace can be logged but must not be the only check. Pair it with executable checks that do not depend on the model's own account.

source: Korbak et al. (2025) Chain of Thought Monitorability: A New and Fragile Opportunity for AI Safety
finding: 41-author position paper: reading reasoning traces gives a useful but imperfect safety signal that may be lost under training pressure.
numbers: No quantitative results in the abstract (41 authors; v1 15 Jul 2025, v2 7 Dec 2025).
limits: Position paper only; abstract read, not the full text.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: supports logging traces as one auditable layer but gives no measured faithfulness rate.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs
finding: No prior work shows self-correction from prompted-LLM feedback, except on tasks unusually suited to it. It works when reliable external feedback exists, and after large-scale fine-tuning.
numbers: Abstract only; no figures. Three findings: prompted self-feedback fails, external feedback works, fine-tuning enables it.
limits: Survey covers mostly 2023-2024 models; abstract read only.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: matches our rule that a check must be external (program, test, second sample), not the same model re-reading its answer.

source: Tsui (2025) Self-Correction Bench: Uncovering and Addressing the Self-Correction Blind Spot in LLMs
finding: Models fix an error placed in the user turn but often not the same error in their own turn. Reasoning-trained models show almost no blind spot. A one-word 'Wait' cue recovers most of it.
numbers: 14 non-reasoning models: average blind spot 64.5%. Claude 3.5 Haiku 52.5%, Claude Sonnet 4 41.4%. BIG-Bench Mistake 62.8%. Wait cuts blind spot 89.3% and lifts accuracy 156% (DeepSeek-V3-0324 0.567 -> 0.902; R1-0528 0.908). R1-Distill-Llama-70B blind spot: -0.031 on GSM8K-SC, -0.050 on PRM800K-SC (base 0.689, 0.317). SFT on 5,306 traces cuts 76.0%. Sets: SCLI5 286, GSM8K-SC 1,313, PRM800K-SC 448; temperature 0, 1,024 tokens.
limits: Errors are injected or taken from other models' outputs, not always the model's own natural slips; 1,024-token cap; math-heavy; open models mainly.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 partly closed: self-checking is not dead on reasoning models, but the test is detection of a given error. Still add an external check; cheap Wait-style re-entry is a free first layer.

source: Kumar et al. (2024) Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe)
finding: Prompted self-correction is described as largely ineffective in modern LLMs; trained with multi-turn RL, it improves.
numbers: Gains of 15.6% and 9.1% on Gemini 1.0 Pro and 1.5 Flash (reported on MATH and HumanEval; abstract does not pair them).
limits: Abstract only; model-specific training, not a prompting scaffold.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: self-correction needs training; a scaffold cannot assume it.

source: Li et al. (2025) ToRL: Scaling Tool-Integrated RL
finding: A real code interpreter in the RL loop beats the same models without it on hard competition math.
numbers: AIME24: Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct no tool 10.0, TIR 13.3, ToRL-1.5B 26.7. 7B: Instruct no tool 10.0, TIR 26.7, SimpleRL-Zero (text RL) 33.3, ToRL-7B 43.3. Code in responses rose from 40% to 80% within 100 steps. Tool calls slowed training: 118 s per step (no calls) to 237 s (C=1) and 288 s (C=2). Raising call limit to 2 added about 2%.
limits: Comparison rows differ in training recipe, so not a clean ablation; math only; no equal-token control; table lacks bare base models.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 partly: on a harder benchmark than GSM8K and on 2025 models, real execution still adds points. Not tested versus a model-simulated check at equal tokens.

source: Li et al. (2023/2024) Chain of Code: Reasoning with a Language Model-Augmented Code Emulator
finding: Code run by a real interpreter reaches near 100% when the code is right. Code-only fails on semantic tasks. Letting the model simulate lines the interpreter cannot run keeps the gain.
numbers: BIG-Bench Hard 23 tasks, single-task prompt: text-davinci-003 direct 55, CoT 72, CoC 84; PaLM-2-S* direct 49, CoT 61, CoC 78. Cross-task: 50 / 55 / 61 and 45 / 47 / 47. GPT-4 CoC 91. Human baseline 68. Python-only ablation fails almost all non-algorithmic tasks; LM-only simulation also does poorly.
limits: Mostly davinci-003 and PaLM-2, 2023 models; ablation figures not read (text only).
agent_relevance: Gap 1: second benchmark family (BBH, not just math) agrees: interpreter where code fits, model for the rest. Use a hybrid, not code for everything.

source: Hu et al. (2025) Evaluating Memory in LLM Agents via Incremental Multi-Turn Interactions (MemoryAgentBench)
finding: An independent benchmark of memory designs shows no memory add-on wins everywhere; long context beats most memory agents, RAG wins mainly on exact retrieval.
numbers: Overall: GPT-5-mini long-context 60.6; Claude-3.7-Sonnet 49.6; GPT-4o 48.8; BM25 RAG 41.5; embedding RAG 29.8-38.2; MemGPT 28.3; MIRIX 26.2 (37.7 with GPT-4.1-mini); Mem0 21.1; Cognee 20.6; Self-RAG 18.7. Accurate retrieval: BM25 60.5 vs GPT-4o-mini backbone 49.2. Selective forgetting: all but GPT-5-mini at or below about 25; multi-hop forgetting at most 28%.
limits: Benchmark is not by the MemGPT or Voyager authors; mixed backbones (RAG on GPT-4o-mini), so not a pure design comparison; second part of the paper not read.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: external memory is not a free gain. Our scratch notes should be simple text/search, long context first, and tested on retrieval and forgetting separately.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Rethinking the Bounds of LLM Reasoning: Are Multi-Agent Discussions the Key?
finding: A single model with a strong prompt nearly matches the best multi-agent discussion; discussion wins only when the prompt has no demonstrations.
numbers: Abstract only; no figures extracted (paper has 10 tables).
limits: Not token-matched in the abstract; 2024 models.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: consistent with Tran and Kiela 2026; the result survives two years of model change.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally Can Be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: The best way to spend test-time compute depends on prompt difficulty. Per-prompt allocation beats best-of-N.
numbers: More than 4x efficiency over a best-of-N baseline; a smaller model can beat a 14x larger one in a FLOPs-matched test on problems where it has non-trivial success.
limits: Abstract only; parallel versus sequential split not read.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: supports a difficulty-based budget rule, not one fixed strategy.

source: arXiv 2506.04210 (2025): extended thinking versus parallel paths at matched budget (authors and title not confirmed)
finding: Longer chains first help, then decline (overthinking). Several independent paths with majority vote beat extended thinking at the same budget.
numbers: Up to 20% higher accuracy for parallel thinking than extended thinking; extended thinking with Wait cues improves then declines.
limits: Abstract summary only; benchmark and model names not read.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: for decomposable or verifiable tasks, cap chain length and vote; fits the difficulty split in Snell and Kim.

source: Kirsh and Maglio (1994) On Distinguishing Epistemic from Pragmatic Action
finding: Tetris players rotate and translate zoids more than needed to place them, and this speeds judgment. Physical rotation takes as little as 100 ms versus about 800-1200 ms estimated for mental rotation.
numbers: Mental rotation pilot: 3 players (intermediate, advanced, expert), 8 presentations of each zoid pair, reaction time rose linearly with angle (0-180 deg). Translate-to-wall-then-drop in about 1% of drops; mean drop distance after routine 19.04, 19.33, 20.05 vs 13.18, 13.69, 15.65 without (all differ, alpha .05). Keystroke gap about 75 ms.
limits: Game logs and a tiny mental-rotation pilot (3 subjects); no independent replication found; descriptive.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 partly: the original numbers are small-sample and descriptive. Epistemic action maps to cheap probe calls (run, test) before committing.

source: Magen and Tomer-Offen (2025) Reduced relational and item-specific processing in cognitive offloading
finding: Recent human result: people who trust an external list remember less internally, for items and for category relations.
numbers: Experiment 1: N=40. Free recall higher without offloading, t(38)=7.22, p<.001, d=2.28. Category access t(38)=5.86, d=1.85; clustering (ARC) t(38)=3.28, p<.01, d=1.04.
limits: Word lists, 30-minute session, small N, between-subject; not a founding-study replication.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: offloading raises dependence on the store. The agent's notes must be organised by relation, not as a flat dump.

source: Kim et al. (2025), power and sample caveats, full text
finding: Per-cell results are noisy; only the aggregate trend supports the architecture rules.
numbers: Per-cell bootstrap CI width about 20 points at n=20; pairwise comparisons underpowered; 8 models x 2 benchmarks aggregate used for the threshold test.
limits: The 87% rule accuracy is for held-out configurations in the authors' own framework.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: treat any threshold as a prior and re-measure on our tasks.
